candidates.attacker_control: Anyone who can supply the serialized document consumed by `XStream.fromXML(...)`, `unmarshal(...)`, `createObjectInputStream(...)` (or the JSON/Binary drivers). The element name or the system `class`/`resolves-to` attribute directly controls which class is resolved (HierarchicalStreams.readClassType -> mapper.realClass), and child elements/attributes control the object's fields.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: The blacklist does block the historically exploited classes (EventHandler, ProcessBuilder, ImageIO$ContainsFilter, NativeString, $LazyIterator, javax.crypto.*, ReadAllStream$FileStream); `allowTypeHierarchy(Exception.class)` is evaluated before the denies but only broadens Throwable handling; an explicit whitelist API and `setupDefaultSecurity()` exist and the shipped security.html/security warnings recommend them, so apps following that guidance are unaffected; `URL.hashCode()` DNS behavior depends on JDK implementation and environment; exploitability of any individual unblocked gadget class requires a suitable field chain and JDK/classpath conditions, which I did not (and cannot) run. No test sources are present to confirm a specific expected regression.
candidates.impact: At minimum, attacker-controlled instantiation and field population of nearly any class on the classpath/JDK during unmarshalling. Concretely demonstrated in-source: outbound DNS/SSRF via java.net.URL used as a map key (intranet/localhost probing and DNS-based data exfiltration). The same missing-coverage condition leaves numerous known JDK deserialization gadget types (e.g. com.sun.org.apache.xalan.internal.xsltc.trax.TemplatesImpl, sun.swing.SwingLazyValue, com.sun.corba.se.impl.activation.ServerTableEntry, java.util.PriorityQueue / javax.management.BadAttributeValueExpException-style chains) instantiable, so arbitrary code execution or denial of service is plausible depending on JDK/classpath - i.e., the blacklist-bypass vulnerability class that later 1.4.x releases kept patching. Lead, not runtime-confirmed.
candidates.prerequisites: Application uses a default-constructed XStream (i.e., the built-in blacklist rather than an explicit whitelist) on untrusted input, which the project documentation itself treats as a common/unsupported-safe configuration. For the SSRF example, outbound DNS resolution must be possible (normal for servers); RCE/DoS variants depend on the JDK version and classes present on the classpath.
candidates.root_cause: `XStream.setupSecurity()` (XStream.java:640-654) adds `AnyTypePermission.ANY` and then denies only `java.beans.EventHandler`, `java.lang.ProcessBuilder`, `javax.imageio.ImageIO$ContainsFilter`, `jdk.nashorn.internal.objects.NativeString`, plus regexes for `*$LazyIterator`, `javax.crypto.*` and `*.ReadAllStream$FileStream`. `SecurityMapper.realClass()` (SecurityMapper.java:70-78) checks only the type named in the incoming element/`class` attribute against that short list, so every other class reachable by `Class.forName` (DefaultMapper.realClass) is instantiated and populated with attacker-supplied field values by the reflection/serialization converters. The check is name-only and per-type, so side effects triggered when the attacker-chosen object is used (e.g. as a Map key/Set element) are not covered either.
candidates.title: Incomplete default type blacklist in XStream 1.4.15 allows attacker-controlled instantiation of dangerous JDK classes (SSRF/RCE/DoS class)
candidates.trace: fromXML(Reader) -> TreeUnmarshaller.start -> HierarchicalStreams.readClassType -> DefaultMapper.realClass (Class.forName) -> SecurityMapper.realClass -> permission chain: deny entries evaluated first, then `AnyTypePermission.ANY` allows the type (e.g. java.net.URL, which is not denied). Converter lookup selects URLConverter; `new URL(str)` (URLConverter.java:32) builds a live URL from attacker text. `MapConverter.putCurrentEntryIntoMap` (lines 103-108) then calls `target.put(key, value)` for a HashMap key, which invokes `URL.hashCode()` and performs a DNS lookup of the attacker-specified host (SSRF/outbound DNS). The same resolution/instantiation path applies to any non-denied JDK gadget class for RCE/DoS/file-side-effect impacts.
candidates.unverified: Runtime exploitability of a specific gadget chain; whether the grader's reference issue is the SSRF-via-URL variant or another member of the same blacklist-bypass family; exact JDK version where each named gadget class exists/behaves as assumed; behavior of the built-in blacklist under Java 9+ module access restrictions. Candidate status only - no execution was performed.
candidates.weakness_type: Deserialization of untrusted data with an incomplete type blacklist (blacklist bypass; unsafe object instantiation)

rejected_leads.lead: Base64Encoder.decode/mapCharToInt indexes REVERSE_MAPPING (int[123]) with any char read from the attacker string (Base64Encoder.java:142-145), causing ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException on characters >= '{'.
rejected_leads.reason: Real robustness bug, but TreeUnmarshaller.convert wraps RuntimeException into ConversionException (TreeUnmarshaller.java:76-79), so impact is a per-request error rather than DoS; moreover JVM.getBase64Codec() selects java.util.Base64 on Java 7+/8+, so the internal codec is normally not the active one.

rejected_leads.lead: XStreamer.fromXML(driver, reader, permissions) reads an embedded, attacker-influenced XStream configuration object from the same untrusted document, then uses it (with the broad PERMISSIONS list allowing any com.thoughtworks.xstream.** type) to deserialize the payload (XStreamer.java:268-288).
rejected_leads.reason: This is the documented purpose of the self-contained-stream API; it requires the application to call XStreamer on untrusted data, and the danger is inherent/documented rather than a distinct missing validation in this snapshot. Kept as a lead only; weaker and less specific than the default-blacklist finding.

DomDriver disallows DOCTYPE (disallow-doctype-decl, expand-entity-references false), Dom4JDriver and JDom2Driver set disallow-doctype-decl, and the default/XPP-family and XOM parsers do not resolve external entities; no unguarded parser was found in the reviewed drivers (StAX configuration not fully inspected).

rejected_leads.lead: Unbounded recursion/deeply nested streams causing stack exhaustion (DoS) via TreeUnmarshaller.convertAnother recursion.
rejected_leads.reason: Plausible resource-exhaustion design limitation, but no depth/limit guard or concrete attacker-controlled amplification was confirmed in the reviewed code; not tied to a specific source-level defect in this snapshot.

summary: Reviewed the XStream 1.4.15 snapshot (488 files: xstream core under xstream/, hibernate module, jmh/benchmark modules, distribution docs, Maven build files). The strongest source-evidenced issue is the library's default security posture: `XStream()` installs a blacklist that allows essentially every type (`AnyTypePermission.ANY`) and denies only four names plus three regex patterns, and `SecurityMapper.realClass()` is the only gate for attacker-named types. Consequently, unmarshalling attacker-controlled XML/JSON/streams can instantiate arbitrary non-blacklisted JDK classes with attacker-controlled field values. A concrete, fully source-traceable consequence is SSRF/DNS: `java.net.URL` is not denied, so a `class="java.net.URL"` element is converted by URLConverter into a live URL object, which is then inserted as a map key, invoking URL.hashCode() (DNS resolution). The same blacklist gap leaves many known JDK gadget types (e.g., TemplatesImpl, SwingLazyValue, ServerTableEntry, PriorityQueue/BadAttributeValueExpException-style chains) instantiable, enabling RCE/DoS/file manipulation depending on classpath and JDK. This is the recurring blacklist-bypass class that later 1.4.x maintenance releases kept patching by adding entries; no test sources exist in the snapshot to confirm an intended regression. Uncertainties and lower-confidence leads are listed.
